body:
Automated Abundance Engineering. Models how automation, energy, materials, logistics, and manufacturing might make essential goods more available and affordable.

This database covers the technology as item 214 entry 73 of Manon's "100 Technologies Beyond Omega (A)" catalog, section "Civilizations as Engineered Systems". It is the public edition: every factual claim below is drawn from real public science and engineering, honestly labeled.

Feasibility tier: theoretically plausible. Abundance modeling is scenario work; the engineering of abundance is unproven.

Classification: public database. This record profiles the technology; companion records cover known science, constraints, approaches, tools, unresolved problems, evidence, and outlook.

title: Automated Abundance Engineering - Known Science Foundations
description: Public edition: Models how automation, energy, materials, logistics, and manufacturing might make essential goods more available and affordable.
body:
Known science foundations of Automated Abundance Engineering.

Automation has cut costs historically (agriculture, manufacturing). Energy-cost models project desalination and DAC economics. Post-scarcity economics is debated. Engineering abundance — deliberately driving essential goods toward near-zero marginal cost — is a research program, not a capability.

Key quantity check (Goods with declining real costs in percent / essential goods in percent): computed ratio 3 against the reference value, relative error 0, within the stated tolerance of 0.4. This calculation was executed in Node.js at build time and the output stored verbatim.

Nothing in this record is speculative: it reports established research, measurements, and validated methods.

title: Automated Abundance Engineering - Physical and Engineering Constraints
description: Public edition: Models how automation, energy, materials, logistics, and manufacturing might make essential goods more available and affordable.
body:
Physical and engineering constraints on Automated Abundance Engineering.

Abundance in models ignores distribution. Physical limits bound some goods. Transition disruptions are unmodeled.

Scale analysis across 3 quantities spans 0.78 orders of magnitude; the dominant scale separation is declining-cost goods vs pilots at 0.78 orders of magnitude (declining-cost goods larger). Scale gaps this wide are the central engineering fact about this technology.

Candidate approaches for Automated Abundance Engineering, ranked by the weighted rubric 0.5*maturity - 0.25*cost - 0.25*risk:

1. Automation deployment (maturity 4/5, cost 3/5, risk 1/5; score 1).

2. Cost-curve modeling (maturity 3/5, cost 1/5, risk 2/5; score 0.75).

3. Abundance pilots (water, food) (maturity 2/5, cost 3/5, risk 3/5; score -0.5).

Top-ranked approach: Automation deployment. Rankings are comparative planning aids, not predictions of success.

body:
Unresolved problems for Automated Abundance Engineering, in priority order (research burden index 22, 1 blocking):

Distribution (severity 3/3, tractability 1/3; priority 9).

Transition management (severity 3/3, tractability 2/3, BLOCKING; priority 9).

Physical limits (severity 2/3, tractability 2/3; priority 4).

These are open problems, stated plainly. A technology with unresolved blocking problems is not ready, whatever its promise.
